paper_context.research_question: How can a suitable evaluation dataset for concept-map-based multi-document summarization be created, given the complexity and lack of existing resources?
main_claims: Concept maps can concisely represent important information and structure large document collections, serving as a valuable variant of multi-document summarization.
A novel crowdsourcing approach, 'low-context importance annotation', can efficiently and reliably determine important elements for concept map summaries in large document collections.
A new corpus of 30 topics, each with around 40 heterogeneous web documents and a summarizing concept map, has been created and released.
The released corpus, along with a baseline system and proposed evaluation protocol, enables further research on concept-map-based multi-document summarization.
The created document clusters are 15 times larger and more heterogeneous than typical DUC clusters, posing a challenging summarization task.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Novelty and utility of the concept-map-based multi-document summarization task.
Soundness and efficiency of the 'low-context importance annotation' crowdsourcing scheme.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Concept maps can be used to concisely represent important information and bring structure into large document collections, serving as a valuable variant of multi-document summarization.
evidence: Concept maps can be used to concisely represent important information and bring structure into large document collections. Therefore, we study a variant of multidocument summarization that produces summaries in the form of concept maps.
Therefore, we believe that the study of summarization with similarly structured outputs is an important extension of the traditional task.

extracted_claims.claim_text: A novel crowdsourcing approach, 'low-context importance annotation', can efficiently and reliably determine important elements for concept map summaries in large document collections.
evidence: It was created using a novel crowdsourcing approach that allows us to efficiently determine important elements in large document collections.
In addition, the method includes a novel crowdsourcing scheme, low-context importance annotation, that resolves quality issues observed in previous work (Lloret et al., 2013).
To overcome these issues, we introduce a new task design, low-context importance annotation, to determine summary-worthy parts of documents.

extracted_claims.claim_text: A new corpus of 30 topics, each with around 40 heterogeneous web documents and a summarizing concept map, has been created and released.
evidence: We present a newly created corpus of concept maps that summarize heterogeneous collections of web documents on educational topics.
For concept-map-based MDS, we created a new corpus of 30 topics, each with around 40 source documents and a summarizing concept map that is the consensus of many crowdworkers.

extracted_claims.claim_text: The released corpus, along with a baseline system and proposed evaluation protocol, enables further research on concept-map-based multi-document summarization.
evidence: We release the corpus along with a baseline system and proposed evaluation protocol to enable further research on this variant of summarization.
These resources are publicly available under a permissive license.

extracted_claims.claim_text: The created document clusters are 15 times larger and more heterogeneous than typical DUC clusters, posing a challenging summarization task.
evidence: Using it, we can avoid the high effort for single annotators, allowing us to scale to document clusters that are 15 times larger than in traditional summarization corpora.
The document clusters were built from a web crawl, comprising a variety of different genres, text styles and document lengths.
With these characteristics, the document clusters are 15 times larger than typical DUC clusters of ten documents and five times larger than the 25-document-clusters (Table 2).
Because we used a large web crawl as the source for our corpus, it contains documents from a variety of genres.
In addition to the variety of genres, the documents also differ in terms of language use.

extracted_claims.claim_text: The low-context importance annotation scheme resolves quality issues observed in previous crowdsourcing work for summarization.
evidence: In addition, the method includes a novel crowdsourcing scheme, low-context importance annotation, that resolves quality issues observed in previous work (Lloret et al., 2013).
To overcome these issues, we introduce a new task design, low-context importance annotation, to determine summary-worthy parts of documents.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Crowdsourcing tasks align with best practices
extracted_claims.claim_text: The proposed crowdsourcing tasks are simple, intuitive, small, and workers receive reasonable payment, aligning with crowdsourcing best practices.
evidence: Compared to Lloret et al.’s approach, it is more in line with crowdsourcing best practices, as the tasks are simple, intuitive and small (Sabou et al., 2014) and workers receive reasonable payment (Fort et al., 2011).

extracted_claims.claim_text: The low-context design, despite minimal context, works reasonably well for importance annotation as long as the topic is relatable to the worker.
evidence: In preliminary tests, we found that this design, despite the minimal context, works reasonably well as long as the topic is something the worker can relate to.

extracted_claims.claim_text: The consensus of multiple workers, represented in the average score, tends to be less subjective than single worker judgments due to the “wisdom of the crowd”.
evidence: This follows the idea that while single workers might find the task subjective, the consensus of multiple workers, represented in the average score, tends to be less subjective due to the “wisdom of the crowd”.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Comparison tasks are easier and more consistent
extracted_claims.claim_text: Comparison tasks are known to be easier to make and more consistent than Likert-scale ratings.
evidence: Comparisons are known to be easier to make and more consistent (Belz and Kow, 2010), but also more expensive, as the number of pairs grows quadratically with the number of objects.

extracted_claims.claim_text: The proposed crowdsourcing scheme allows for the collection of reliable annotations for proposition importance, both on TAC documents and the new dataset.
evidence: This shows that the approach, despite the high subjectiveness of the task, allows us to collect reliable annotations.
These figures show that the crowdsourcing approach works on this dataset as reliably as on the TAC documents.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Importance annotations useful for summary evaluation
extracted_claims.claim_text: The obtained importance annotations are similarly useful for summary evaluation as pyramid annotations or ROUGE scores from gold-standard summaries.
evidence: The results demonstrate that with both task designs, we obtain importance annotations that are similarly useful for summary evaluation as pyramid annotations or gold-standard summaries (used for ROUGE).

extracted_claims.claim_text: The presented corpus construction process efficiently creates the dataset by combining automatic preprocessing, scalable crowdsourcing, and high-quality expert annotations.
evidence: We present our corpus construction process, outlined in Figure 4, that combines automatic preprocessing, scalable crowdsourcing and high-quality expert annotations to efficiently create such a dataset.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Open IE 4 is a state-of-the-art Open Information Extraction system.
evidence: We used Open IE 47, a state-of-the-art Open IE system (Stanovsky and Dagan, 2016), to process the relevant sentences of all topics.

extracted_claims.claim_label: SVM classifier for proposition filtering is effective
extracted_claims.claim_text: A linear SVM classifier, tuned to avoid false negatives, effectively filters unsuitable propositions while maintaining high precision on negative classifications.
evidence: Under these constraints, a model trained on 350 instances achieves 93% precision on negative classifications on the unseen 150 instances, assuming that 20% are manually verified.
uncertainty_flags: Requires manual verification for a subset of classifications.

extracted_claims.claim_text: The expert annotation steps for concept map construction (proposition selection, concept joining, concept labeling) show substantial inter-annotator agreement.
evidence: We casted the task of selecting propositions to be included in the map as a binary decision task and observed an agreement of 84% (κ = 0.66).
Second, we modeled the decision which concepts to join as a binary decision on all pairs of common concepts, observing an agreement of 95% (κ = 0.70).

And finally, we compared which concept labels the annotators decided to include in the final map, observing 85% (κ = 0.69) agreement. Hence, the annotation shows substantial agreement (Landis and Koch, 1977).

extracted_claims.claim_text: Analysis of the baseline system reveals major bottlenecks and challenges for concept-map-based MDS, particularly in content selection and relation extraction.
evidence: An analysis of the single pipeline steps revealed major bottlenecks of the method and challenges of the task.

First, we observed that around 76% of gold concepts are covered with the extraction (step 1+2), while the top 25 concepts (step 5) only contain 17%. Hence, content selection is a major challenge, stemming from the large cluster sizes.
Second, while also 17% of gold concepts are contained in the final maps (step 6), scores for strict proposition matching are low, indicating a poor performance of the relation extraction (step 3).

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Concept maps are a valuable and useful output format for multi-document summarization, aligning with human information-seeking behavior.
supporting_evidence: Instead, user studies (Chin et al., 2009; Kang et al., 2011) show that they note down important keywords and phrases, try to identify relationships between them and organize them accordingly. Therefore, we believe that the study of summarization with similarly structured outputs is an important extension of the traditional task.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: The fundamental utility and relevance of the proposed task (concept-map-based MDS) would be undermined.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Focusing on an extractive variant of concept-map-based MDS, where all labels are taken from documents, is sufficient to ease automatic evaluation without compromising task utility.
supporting_evidence: Further, to ease the use of automatic evaluations, we focus on the extractive variant of the task in this work, requiring that all labels have to be taken from the documents.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Automatic evaluation might not fully capture the nuances or potential benefits of abstractive concept map summarization, or the extractive constraint might limit the expressiveness of summaries.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Open Information Extraction (Open IE) tuples provide a suitable and sufficiently accurate structural representation (concepts and relations) to serve as a starting point for concept map propositions.
supporting_evidence: As concept maps consist of propositions expressing the relation between concepts (see Figure 1), we need to impose such a structure upon the plain text in the document clusters... Therefore, we resort to an automatic approach for this step. The Open Information Extraction paradigm (Banko et al., 2007) offers a representation very similar to the desired one.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Errors or limitations in Open IE extraction would propagate through the entire corpus creation pipeline, affecting the quality and validity of the gold-standard concept maps.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The confidence scores assigned by Open IE 4 are reliable indicators of extraction quality and can be effectively used for filtering low-quality propositions.
supporting_evidence: We therefore made use of the confidence assigned to every extracted tuple to filter out low quality ones.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Ineffective filtering based on confidence scores could lead to either too many low-quality propositions or the loss of important, but low-confidence, propositions.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The 'low-context importance annotation' scheme, which provides only a topic description, is a valid method for crowdworkers to accurately determine the importance of propositions for a summary.
supporting_evidence: The goal of our crowdsourcing scheme is to obtain a score for each proposition indicating its importance in a document cluster, such that a ranking according to the score would reveal what is most important and should be included in a summary.
In contrast to other work, we do not show the documents to the workers at all, but provide only a description of the document cluster’s topic.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: The importance scores derived from crowdsourcing might not accurately reflect the true importance of propositions, leading to a flawed gold standard for summarization.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The 'wisdom of the crowd' principle, applied through averaging Likert scores or TrueSkill rankings, effectively mitigates the inherent subjectivity of importance annotation to produce reliable estimates.
supporting_evidence: This follows the idea that while single workers might find the task subjective, the consensus of multiple workers, represented in the average score, tends to be less subjective due to the “wisdom of the crowd”.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If collective judgments do not sufficiently overcome individual subjectivity, the resulting importance scores could still be biased or inconsistent, impacting the quality of the gold standard.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The quality control measures implemented for crowdsourcing (US workers, approval rate, correlation checks, trap sentences) are sufficient to ensure high-quality annotations.
supporting_evidence: Following the observations of Lloret et al. (2013), we established several measures for quality control. First, we restricted our tasks to workers from the US with an approval rate of at least 95%. Second, we identified low quality workers by measuring the correlation of each worker’s Likert-scores with the average of the other four scores. ... In addition, we included trap sentences...
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If low-quality workers or malicious behavior is not adequately filtered, the crowdsourced importance annotations could be compromised, affecting the gold standard's reliability.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The SVM classifier for proposition filtering, despite requiring manual verification for some cases, maintains sufficient data quality by prioritizing the avoidance of false negatives.
supporting_evidence: To ensure that the automatic classification does not remove suitable propositions, we tuned the classifier to avoid false negatives. In particular, we introduced class weights, improving precision on the negative class at the cost of a higher fraction of positive classifications. Further, we assumed that we can manually verify a certain number of the most uncertain negative classifications.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: The trade-off might lead to a higher number of unsuitable propositions remaining in the dataset, increasing expert annotation effort, or the manual verification process might introduce new biases or inconsistencies.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The selection of the top 50 propositions per topic from the crowdsourced ranking is an appropriate threshold for constructing a comprehensive and high-quality summary concept map.
supporting_evidence: From the fine-grained ranking of the 100 most important propositions, we select the top 50 per topic to construct a summary concept map in the subsequent steps.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Too few propositions might lead to incomplete summaries, while too many might introduce less important information or make the expert annotation process overly complex.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Expert annotators can consistently and accurately perform the complex tasks of proposition revision and concept map construction, including concept joining and relation selection, to create high-quality gold-standard maps.
supporting_evidence: Having a manageable number of propositions per topic, an expert annotator then applied a few straightforward transformations that correct common errors of the Open IE system.
As these decisions highly depend upon each other and require context, we decided to use expert annotators rather than crowdsource the subtasks.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Inconsistencies or errors in expert annotations would directly compromise the quality and reliability of the gold-standard concept maps, affecting subsequent system evaluations.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: A target size of 25 concepts is an appropriate and recommended maximum size for a summary concept map, balancing conciseness and informativeness.
supporting_evidence: They were instructed to reach a size of 25 concepts, the recommended maximum size for a concept map (Novak and Cañas, 2007).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If 25 concepts is not an optimal size, the resulting summaries might be either too sparse or too dense, potentially limiting their utility or representativeness.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Allowing up to three synthetic relations, which makes the maps 'slightly abstractive', does not fundamentally compromise the 'extractive variant' nature of the task or the integrity of the gold standard.
supporting_evidence: If an annotator was not able to connect 25 concepts, she was allowed to create up to three synthetic relations with freely defined labels, making the maps slightly abstractive.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: The introduction of abstractive elements could complicate the evaluation of purely extractive systems or introduce a mismatch with the stated goal of focusing on an extractive task for automatic evaluation.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The proposed automatic evaluation metrics (Strict Match, METEOR, ROUGE-2) are sufficient and appropriate for comparing generated concept maps with reference maps.
supporting_evidence: In order to automatically compare generated concept maps with reference maps, we propose three metrics. ... These automatic measures might be complemented with a human evaluation.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If these metrics do not adequately capture the quality, coherence, or informativeness of concept maps, system development might be misdirected, or true performance differences might be obscured.

argument_focus: Problem identification: Lack of suitable evaluation datasets for concept-map-based multi-document summarization.
Method development: Creation of a novel crowdsourcing approach ('low-context importance annotation') and a multi-stage corpus construction pipeline.
Resource creation: Development and release of a new corpus of concept maps, a baseline system, and an evaluation protocol.
Empirical validation: Pilot study on crowdsourcing reliability, corpus analysis, and baseline experiments to demonstrate task challenges.
contribution_targets: Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, specifically in summarization and knowledge representation.
Researchers working on multi-document summarization, by providing a new task, dataset, and evaluation framework.
Researchers interested in crowdsourcing methodologies for complex annotation tasks.
Educational technology and information retrieval, by offering a new way to structure and navigate large document collections.
evaluation_targets: Novelty and utility of the concept-map-based multi-document summarization task itself.
Soundness, efficiency, and reliability of the 'low-context importance annotation' crowdsourcing scheme.
Quality, size, representativeness, and generalizability of the created concept map corpus.
Clarity, completeness, and appropriateness of the provided evaluation protocol and baseline system.
Potential impact and advancement of research in multi-document summarization and knowledge representation.
uncertainty_flags: The effectiveness of the 'low-context' crowdsourcing design relies on workers' ability to relate to the topic without full document context, which might vary.
Comparison tasks are acknowledged to be more expensive, implying a trade-off between consistency and cost.

The SVM classifier for proposition filtering was tuned to avoid false negatives, which might lead to a higher fraction of positive classifications requiring manual verification, indicating a limitation in full automation.

Manual correction was performed for 'least confident negative classifications' and 'positive classifications for certain types of tuples' where the classifier was imprecise, highlighting the limits of the automatic filtering.
The decision to limit connections in concept maps to avoid compromising importance suggests a potential trade-off in graph density or completeness.
The allowance for 'up to three synthetic relations' makes the maps 'slightly abstractive', which could introduce a tension with the stated focus on an 'extractive variant' for automatic evaluation.
The proposed automatic evaluation measures 'might be complemented with a human evaluation', indicating that their comprehensiveness or validity might be limited on their own.
chaining_notes: Downstream reviewers should critically assess the validity of the 'low-context importance annotation' methodology, particularly the assumption that crowdworkers can reliably judge proposition importance without access to the full source documents.

The trade-offs made during the corpus creation pipeline, such as the SVM classifier's tuning to avoid false negatives and the allowance for 'slightly abstractive' synthetic relations, warrant close examination for their impact on gold-standard quality and task definition.
The generalizability of the crowdsourcing reliability results (from TAC documents) to the new corpus's larger, more heterogeneous web document clusters should be considered.
The suitability and comprehensiveness of the proposed automatic evaluation metrics for concept maps need to be thoroughly evaluated, especially given the note that human evaluation might be needed.
The consistency between the stated focus on an 'extractive variant' of the task and the inclusion of 'slightly abstractive' elements in the gold standard should be reconciled.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes a novel task: concept-map-based multi-document summarization (MDS). It addresses the lack of suitable evaluation datasets by presenting a new corpus, created through a multi-stage pipeline combining automatic preprocessing, a novel 'low-context importance annotation' crowdsourcing scheme, and expert annotation. The paper logically argues for the utility of concept maps as a summary format, validates its crowdsourcing method through a pilot study, details the corpus construction, characterizes the resulting large and heterogeneous dataset, and provides a baseline system and evaluation protocol. The overall argument flow is coherent, moving from problem identification to a detailed solution and its empirical validation, aiming to enable future research in this new summarization paradigm.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Traditional MDS outputs (text summaries) do not fully align with human information-seeking behavior for large document collections (Section 1).
C1: Concept maps offer a valuable alternative, concisely representing important information and structuring document collections (Section 1).
P2: A suitable evaluation dataset for concept-map-based MDS is currently missing, hindering research (Section 1).
S1: The paper proposes a novel corpus creation method combining automatic preprocessing, scalable crowdsourcing, and high-quality expert annotations (Section 1, C13).
S2: A key component of S1 is a novel 'low-context importance annotation' crowdsourcing scheme (Section 1, C2, C6).
E1: This crowdsourcing scheme is designed to be efficient and reliable, adhering to best practices (Section 3, C7).
E2: A pilot study on TAC data demonstrates the reliability and utility of the crowdsourcing scheme for importance annotation (Section 3.2, C11, C12).

S3: The corpus creation pipeline involves: Proposition Extraction (using Open IE 4, C14), Proposition Filtering (using an SVM classifier, C15), Importance Annotation (using the validated crowdsourcing scheme, C11), Proposition Revision (expert correction), and Concept Map Construction (expert annotation, C16) (Section 4).
C3: A new corpus of 30 topics, each with ~40 heterogeneous web documents and a summarizing concept map, has been created and released (Section 1, Section 4).
C5: This corpus features document clusters 15 times larger and more heterogeneous than typical DUC clusters, posing a challenging summarization task (Section 1, Section 5.1).
C4: The released corpus, along with a baseline system and proposed evaluation protocol, enables further research on concept-map-based MDS (Section 1, Section 6).
C17: Analysis of the baseline system reveals major bottlenecks in content selection and relation extraction, highlighting task challenges (Section 6).

concerns.title: Inconsistency in Extractive vs. Abstractive Task Definition
concerns.description: The paper explicitly states a focus on an 'extractive variant' of concept-map-based MDS to ease automatic evaluation (Assumption A2). However, during expert annotation for gold-standard concept maps, annotators were allowed to create 'up to three synthetic relations with freely defined labels, making the maps slightly abstractive' (Assumption A12). This introduces a logical inconsistency between the stated task definition and the nature of the gold standard, potentially complicating the evaluation of purely extractive systems.
evidence: Section 1: 'Further, to ease the use of automatic evaluations, we focus on the extractive variant of the task in this work, requiring that all labels have to be taken from the documents.'
Section 4.6: 'If an annotator was not able to connect 25 concepts, she was allowed to create up to three synthetic relations with freely defined labels, making the maps slightly abstractive.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify the precise definition of the task, either by strictly enforcing an extractive gold standard or by explicitly acknowledging and justifying the 'slightly abstractive' elements as part of the task's scope, and discuss its implications for evaluation.

concerns.title: Validity of 'Low-Context' Importance Annotation
concerns.description: While the pilot study demonstrates reliability (C11), the fundamental assumption (A5) that crowdworkers can accurately and consistently judge the importance of propositions for a summary without access to the full source documents remains a critical point. The justification that it 'works reasonably well as long as the topic is something the worker can relate to' (C8) is somewhat subjective and might not hold universally, potentially introducing biases or limiting the depth of importance assessment.
evidence: Section 3.1: 'In contrast to other work, we do not show the documents to the workers at all, but provide only a description of the document cluster’s topic.'
Section 3.1: 'In preliminary tests, we found that this design, despite the minimal context, works reasonably well as long as the topic is something the worker can relate to.'

Assumption A5: The 'low-context importance annotation' scheme, which provides only a topic description, is a valid method for crowdworkers to accurately determine the importance of propositions for a summary.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a more robust theoretical or empirical justification for the 'low-context' approach's validity, perhaps by comparing low-context annotations with a subset of high-context (full document) annotations, or by analyzing cases where worker relatability might be low.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper introduces a novel task: concept-map-based multi-document summarization (MDS) and a corresponding corpus. The methodology for corpus creation is a multi-stage pipeline combining automatic Open Information Extraction (Open IE), a novel 'low-context importance annotation' crowdsourcing scheme, and expert human annotation. The core reasoning is that concept maps are a valuable summary format, and a hybrid approach can efficiently create a high-quality gold standard for large, heterogeneous document collections. The paper validates individual steps with inter-annotator agreement and pilot studies. While the overall pipeline is well-structured with robust quality control for expert stages, the validity of the low-context crowdsourcing without full document context and the consistency of the 'extractive variant' task definition with the actual gold standard introduce methodological concerns. The proposed automatic evaluation metrics are also acknowledged as potentially incomplete for structured output.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Multi-document summarization (MDS) is a long-studied problem, but traditional textual summaries may not align with human information-seeking behavior (Section 1).
P2: Concept maps offer a structured output that aligns with human information-seeking, can concisely represent important information, and structure large document collections (Section 1, C1).
P3: There is a lack of suitable evaluation datasets for concept-map-based MDS, especially for large, heterogeneous document collections, and manual creation is time-consuming (Section 1).
P4: A novel corpus creation method is needed that combines automatic preprocessing, scalable crowdsourcing, and high-quality expert annotations to efficiently create such a dataset (Section 1, C13).
P5: Open Information Extraction (Open IE) can be used to extract propositions (concept-relation-concept tuples) from documents as a starting point for concept maps (Section 4.2, A3).
P6: Raw Open IE extractions contain noise and unsuitable propositions, requiring filtering (Section 4.2, Section 4.3).

P7: A novel 'low-context importance annotation' crowdsourcing scheme can efficiently and reliably determine the importance of propositions without full document context (Section 1, Section 3, C2, C6, C8, A5, A6).
P8: Quality control measures and 'wisdom of the crowd' mitigate subjectivity and ensure reliability in crowdsourcing (Section 3.2, C7, C9, A6, A7).
P9: Expert annotators are required for complex, context-dependent tasks like proposition revision and final concept map construction to ensure high quality (Section 4.5, Section 4.6, A10).
P10: Inter-annotator agreement for expert tasks demonstrates reliability of the gold standard concept maps (Section 4.6, C16, A10).

P11: The resulting corpus consists of 30 topics with around 40 heterogeneous web documents and summarizing concept maps, which are 15 times larger and more heterogeneous than typical DUC clusters (Section 1, C3, C5).
P12: The released corpus, along with a baseline system and evaluation protocol, enables further research on concept-map-based MDS (Section 1, C4).
P13: Analysis of the baseline system reveals major bottlenecks in content selection and relation extraction, highlighting the challenges of the task (Section 6, C17).
C: Therefore, a new corpus for concept-map-based MDS has been successfully created using a hybrid methodology, providing a benchmark for future research.

The document clusters were built from a web crawl, comprising a variety of different genres, text styles and document lengths.
With these characteristics, the document clusters are 15 times larger than typical DUC clusters of ten documents and five times larger than the 25-document-clusters (Table 2).
Because we used a large web crawl as the source for our corpus, it contains documents from a variety of genres.
In addition to the variety of genres, the documents also differ in terms of language use.

To overcome these issues, we introduce a new task design, low-context importance annotation, to determine summary-worthy parts of documents.

identified_claims.claim_text: The obtained importance annotations are similarly useful for summary evaluation as pyramid annotations or ROUGE scores from gold-standard summaries.

identified_claims.claim_text: The presented corpus construction process efficiently creates the dataset by combining automatic preprocessing, scalable crowdsourcing, and high-quality expert annotations.
evidence: We present our corpus construction process, outlined in Figure 4, that combines automatic preprocessing, scalable crowdsourcing and high-quality expert annotations to efficiently create such a dataset.

identified_claims.claim_text: Open IE 4 is a state-of-the-art Open Information Extraction system.
evidence: We used Open IE 47, a state-of-the-art Open IE system (Stanovsky and Dagan, 2016), to process the relevant sentences of all topics.

identified_claims.claim_label: SVM classifier for proposition filtering is effective
identified_claims.claim_text: A linear SVM classifier, tuned to avoid false negatives, effectively filters unsuitable propositions while maintaining high precision on negative classifications.
evidence: Under these constraints, a model trained on 350 instances achieves 93% precision on negative classifications on the unseen 150 instances, assuming that 20% are manually verified.
uncertainty_flags: Requires manual verification for a subset of classifications.

identified_claims.claim_text: The expert annotation steps for concept map construction (proposition selection, concept joining, concept labeling) show substantial inter-annotator agreement.
evidence: We casted the task of selecting propositions to be included in the map as a binary decision task and observed an agreement of 84% (κ = 0.66).
Second, we modeled the decision which concepts to join as a binary decision on all pairs of common concepts, observing an agreement of 95% (κ = 0.70).

And finally, we compared which concept labels the annotators decided to include in the final map, observing 85% (κ = 0.69) agreement. Hence, the annotation shows substantial agreement (Landis and Koch, 1977).

identified_claims.claim_text: Analysis of the baseline system reveals major bottlenecks and challenges for concept-map-based MDS, particularly in content selection and relation extraction.
evidence: An analysis of the single pipeline steps revealed major bottlenecks of the method and challenges of the task.

First, we observed that around 76% of gold concepts are covered with the extraction (step 1+2), while the top 25 concepts (step 5) only contain 17%. Hence, content selection is a major challenge, stemming from the large cluster sizes.
Second, while also 17% of gold concepts are contained in the final maps (step 6), scores for strict proposition matching are low, indicating a poor performance of the relation extraction (step 3).

strengths.description: The paper proposes a well-justified novel task of concept-map-based multi-document summarization and creates a large, heterogeneous corpus that addresses a clear gap in existing resources. The corpus characteristics (15x larger, more diverse than DUC) make it a challenging and valuable benchmark.

P11: The resulting corpus consists of 30 topics with around 40 heterogeneous web documents and summarizing concept maps, which are 15 times larger and more heterogeneous than typical DUC clusters (Section 1, C3, C5).

strengths.title: Robust Hybrid Corpus Creation Methodology
strengths.description: The multi-stage pipeline, combining automatic extraction, scalable crowdsourcing, and high-quality expert annotation, is a sound approach to manage the complexity and scale of creating structured summaries. The explicit quality control measures at each stage, including manual verification and expert revision, enhance the overall data quality.
evidence: P4: A novel corpus creation method is needed that combines automatic preprocessing, scalable crowdsourcing, and high-quality expert annotations to efficiently create such a dataset (Section 1, C13).
P9: Expert annotators are required for complex, context-dependent tasks like proposition revision and final concept map construction to ensure high quality (Section 4.5, Section 4.6, A10).
P8: Quality control measures and 'wisdom of the crowd' mitigate subjectivity and ensure reliability in crowdsourcing (Section 3.2, C7, C9, A6, A7).
A8: The SVM classifier for proposition filtering, despite manual verification, maintains sufficient data quality by prioritizing the avoidance of false negatives.

strengths.title: High Reliability of Expert Annotation
strengths.description: The inter-annotator agreement for the complex expert annotation steps (proposition selection, concept joining, concept labeling) is substantial (Kappa values 0.66-0.70). This provides strong evidence for the consistency and reliability of the gold-standard concept maps.
evidence: P10: Inter-annotator agreement for expert tasks demonstrates reliability of the gold standard concept maps (Section 4.6, C16, A10).
C16: The expert annotation steps for concept map construction (proposition selection, concept joining, concept labeling) show substantial inter-annotator agreement.

strengths.title: Publicly Available Resources for Reproducibility
strengths.description: The commitment to release the corpus, baseline system, and evaluation scripts under a permissive license is excellent for promoting reproducibility and facilitating future research in this new area.
evidence: P12: The released corpus, along with a baseline system and evaluation protocol, enables further research on concept-map-based MDS (Section 1, C4).
C4: The released corpus, along with a baseline system and proposed evaluation protocol, enables further research on concept-map-based multi-document summarization.

concerns.title: Unvalidated Validity of Low-Context Importance Annotation
concerns.description: The core assumption (A5) that crowdworkers can accurately judge the importance of propositions for a summary without access to the full source documents is a significant methodological risk. While the pilot study demonstrates consistency (reliability) among workers, it does not rigorously validate the *accuracy* or *validity* of these judgments against an objective truth or expert judgments made with full context. Workers might rely on general knowledge rather than document-specific salience, potentially leading to a gold standard that doesn't truly reflect importance within the given document cluster.
evidence: A5: The 'low-context importance annotation' scheme, which provides only a topic description, is a valid method for crowdworkers to accurately determine the importance of propositions for a summary.

P7: A novel 'low-context importance annotation' crowdsourcing scheme can efficiently and reliably determine the importance of propositions without full document context (Section 1, Section 3, C2, C6, C8, A5, A6).
C8: The low-context design, despite minimal context, works reasonably well for importance annotation as long as the topic is relatable to the worker.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct a targeted study comparing low-context crowd judgments with expert judgments made with full document context for a subset of propositions. Quantify the agreement and correlation to validate the accuracy of the low-context approach.

concerns.title: Inconsistency in Task Definition (Extractive vs. Abstractive)
concerns.description: The paper explicitly states a focus on the 'extractive variant' of concept-map-based MDS to ease automatic evaluation (A2). However, in the expert annotation stage, annotators are allowed to create 'up to three synthetic relations with freely defined labels, making the maps slightly abstractive' (A12). This introduces a direct inconsistency between the stated task definition and the gold standard, potentially penalizing purely extractive systems that adhere to the initial constraint and complicating evaluation.
evidence: A2: Focusing on an extractive variant of concept-map-based MDS, where all labels are taken from documents, is sufficient to ease automatic evaluation without compromising task utility.

A12: Allowing up to three synthetic relations, which makes the maps 'slightly abstractive', does not fundamentally compromise the 'extractive variant' nature of the task or the integrity of the gold standard.
Section 4.6: If an annotator was not able to connect 25 concepts, she was allowed to create up to three synthetic relations with freely defined labels, making the maps slightly abstractive.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either strictly adhere to a purely extractive gold standard, or explicitly define the task as 'hybrid extractive-abstractive' and provide clear guidelines for how systems should handle or be evaluated on abstractive elements.

concerns.title: Limited Scope of Automatic Evaluation Metrics
concerns.description: The proposed automatic evaluation metrics (Strict Match, METEOR, ROUGE-2) are primarily based on lexical overlap and proposition matching. While useful, they may not fully capture the structural quality, coherence, connectivity, or deeper semantic correctness of concept maps as structured knowledge representations. The paper acknowledges this by stating these measures 'might be complemented with a human evaluation' (A13), indicating their inherent limitations for this complex structured output.
evidence: A13: The proposed automatic evaluation metrics (Strict Match, METEOR, ROUGE-2) are sufficient and appropriate for comparing generated concept maps with reference maps.
Section 6: These automatic measures might be complemented with a human evaluation.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Explore and propose additional evaluation metrics that specifically assess the graph structure, such as graph edit distance, structural similarity measures, or metrics that evaluate the semantic coherence and connectivity of concepts and relations within the map.

concerns.title: Arbitrary Threshold for Proposition Selection
concerns.description: The decision to select the top 50 propositions per topic from the crowdsourced ranking for expert annotation (A9) appears to be an arbitrary threshold. While practical for managing expert workload, the paper does not provide a strong justification for why 50 is optimal in terms of capturing comprehensive summary content or balancing conciseness. This choice could impact the completeness or focus of the resulting gold-standard concept maps.
evidence: A9: The selection of the top 50 propositions per topic from the crowdsourced ranking is an appropriate threshold for constructing a comprehensive and high-quality summary concept map.
Section 4.4: From the fine-grained ranking of the 100 most important propositions, we select the top 50 per topic to construct a summary concept map in the subsequent steps.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a sensitivity analysis or a more explicit rationale for the choice of 50 propositions, perhaps by evaluating the impact of different thresholds on summary quality or coverage.

concerns.title: Generalizability of Crowdsourcing Pilot Study
concerns.description: The pilot study for the 'low-context importance annotation' was conducted on TAC2008 documents, which are typically news articles and less heterogeneous than the web documents in the new corpus. While the study showed reliability on TAC data, the generalizability of the approach's effectiveness (especially the validity of importance judgments without context) to the new corpus's much larger and more diverse web document clusters is assumed rather than explicitly re-validated for accuracy. The 'relatability' of topics (C8) might differ significantly.
evidence: C11: The proposed crowdsourcing scheme allows for the collection of reliable annotations for proposition importance, both on TAC documents and the new dataset.
C5: The created document clusters are 15 times larger and more heterogeneous than typical DUC clusters, posing a challenging summarization task.
Section 3.2: To verify the proposed approach, we conducted a pilot study on Amazon Mechanical Turk using data from TAC2008 (Dang and Owczarzak, 2008).
Section 4.4: These figures show that the crowdsourcing approach works on this dataset as reliably as on the TAC documents.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a more in-depth analysis or a small-scale validation of the low-context importance annotation specifically on the new corpus's heterogeneous web documents, focusing on the agreement with expert judgments (if available) or a qualitative assessment of judgment quality.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The concept-map-based MDS task itself, especially with large and heterogeneous document clusters, represents a significant conceptual divergence from traditional textual summarization. The 'low-context importance annotation' is a novel crowdsourcing methodology. These aspects signal innovation. However, the methodological concerns raised (M1, M2, M3) pertain to the *validity* and *consistency* of these novel methods and definitions, not their inherent novelty. For instance, the novelty of low-context annotation is acknowledged, but its soundness for accurate importance judgment without document context is questioned.

The task definition would be more robust if the 'extractive variant' was either strictly enforced in the gold standard or if the abstractive elements were explicitly modeled and evaluated within a hybrid task framework.
The evaluation framework would be more comprehensive if it included metrics that explicitly assess the structural and semantic coherence of concept maps, beyond lexical overlap.

confidence_interval.rationale: My confidence in this review is high because the paper provides a detailed methodology, allowing for a thorough step-by-step audit of assumptions, model choices, and evaluation setup. The explicit identification of assumptions in the shared analysis was very helpful. While there are significant methodological concerns, the paper's transparency about its methods and limitations, along with the provision of reproducibility resources, allows for a confident assessment of its strengths and weaknesses. The creativity safeguards were applied to distinguish between innovative aspects and methodological flaws.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes concept-map-based multi-document summarization (MDS) as an extension of traditional MDS, motivated by observed human information-seeking behaviors. Its primary contribution is the creation and release of a novel, large-scale, and heterogeneous corpus for this task, accompanied by a baseline system and an evaluation protocol. The corpus construction methodology is a multi-stage pipeline that incrementally refines existing practices by combining automatic Open Information Extraction (Open IE), a novel 'low-context importance annotation' crowdsourcing scheme, and expert revision. This crowdsourcing method is presented as an improvement over prior work by simplifying tasks and aggregating crowd wisdom to address known quality issues. The resulting dataset offers document clusters that are significantly larger and more diverse than established benchmarks like DUC and TAC, thereby posing new challenges for summarization research. The paper effectively extends the summarization paradigm by introducing a structured output format and provides a refined, scalable methodology for complex dataset creation.
logical_argument_graph: Traditional Multi-Document Summarization (MDS) primarily yields textual summaries.
User studies indicate that humans often organize information by noting keywords, phrases, and their relationships, rather than writing full summaries.
Concept maps, as labeled graphs showing concepts and relations, align with this human information organization behavior and offer structured, navigable summaries.
Therefore, concept-map-based MDS is a valuable and important extension of the traditional summarization task (Claim C1).
Effective development and evaluation of methods for concept-map-based MDS necessitate the availability of gold-standard corpora.

Existing summarization corpora are generally unsuitable due to limitations such as focusing on single documents, smaller scale, lack of public availability, or not emphasizing the summarization aspect for concept maps.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes a novel task, concept-map-based multi-document summarization (MDS), arguing that concept maps offer a more intuitive and structured summary format aligned with human information-seeking behavior than traditional text summaries. To enable research in this new paradigm, the authors introduce a comprehensive corpus creation methodology. This multi-stage process integrates automatic Open Information Extraction (Open IE) for initial proposition generation, a novel 'low-context importance annotation' crowdsourcing scheme for efficient importance scoring of propositions, and expert annotation for final concept map construction and refinement. A key feature of the created corpus is its scale and heterogeneity, comprising 30 topics with large, diverse web document clusters, significantly surpassing traditional summarization datasets. The paper also provides a baseline system and an evaluation protocol, aiming to establish a foundation for future research in this distinct summarization approach.
logical_argument_graph: Problem: Traditional MDS outputs (linear text summaries) do not fully align with human information-seeking behavior, which often involves identifying keywords, relationships, and structure. There is a lack of suitable evaluation datasets for structured summarization outputs.

Proposed Novel Task: Introduce Concept-Map-Based MDS, where summaries are represented as concept maps (nodes for concepts, edges for relations). This format offers concise, relational summaries and potential navigation capabilities within document collections.

Challenge for New Task: Creating gold-standard concept map datasets is inherently complex, time-consuming, and difficult to scale, especially for large and heterogeneous document collections. Existing related work and corpora are insufficient (e.g., single-document focus, smaller scale, less compression, or not publicly available).

Proposed Novel Methodology: Develop a multi-stage corpus creation pipeline to address the data scarcity for this complex task. This pipeline includes: (1) Automatic Proposition Extraction using Open IE 4, (2) Automated Proposition Filtering via an SVM classifier, (3) a novel 'Low-Context Importance Annotation' crowdsourcing scheme (using Likert-scale and comparison tasks where workers only see a topic description, not full documents), and (4) Expert Proposition Revision and Concept Map Construction (involving concept joining, relation selection, and adherence to connectedness and size constraints).

Validation of Methodology: A pilot study on TAC data demonstrates the reliability of the crowdsourcing approach and its utility for summary evaluation. Expert annotator agreement for the concept map construction steps is reported as substantial. The resulting corpus's characteristics (size, document heterogeneity) are quantitatively shown to be significantly greater than those of traditional summarization corpora.

Core Contribution: The paper delivers a new corpus of 30 topics, each with approximately 40 source documents and a summarizing concept map. It also provides a baseline system and a proposed evaluation protocol, all publicly available.

Anticipated Impact: These resources are intended to enable and facilitate further research on concept-map-based MDS, providing a challenging benchmark that highlights key bottlenecks (e.g., content selection, relation extraction) and advances the field of multi-document summarization and knowledge representation.

The paper introduces a novel task: concept-map-based multi-document summarization (MDS) and a corresponding corpus. The methodology for corpus creation is a multi-stage pipeline combining automatic Open Information Extraction (Open IE), a novel 'low-context importance annotation' crowdsourcing scheme, and expert human annotation. The core reasoning is that concept maps are a valuable summary format, and a hybrid approach can efficiently create a high-quality gold standard for large, heterogeneous document collections. The paper validates individual steps with inter-annotator agreement and pilot studies. While the overall pipeline is well-structured with robust quality control for expert stages, the validity of the low-context crowdsourcing without full document context and the consistency of the 'extractive variant' task definition with the actual gold standard introduce methodological concerns. The manuscript proposes concept-map-based multi-document summarization (MDS) as an extension of traditional MDS, motivated by observed human information-seeking behaviors. Its primary contribution is the creation and release of a novel, large-scale, and heterogeneous corpus for this task, accompanied by a baseline system and an evaluation protocol. The corpus construction methodology is a multi-stage pipeline that incrementally refines existing practices by combining automatic Open Information Extraction (Open IE), a novel 'low-context importance annotation' crowdsourcing scheme, and expert revision. This crowdsourcing method is presented as an improvement over prior work by simplifying tasks and aggregating crowd wisdom to address known quality issues. The resulting dataset offers document clusters that are significantly larger and more diverse than established benchmarks like DUC and TAC, thereby posing new challenges for summarization research. The paper effectively extends the summarization paradigm by introducing a structured output format and provides a refined, scalable methodology for complex dataset creation.

The manuscript proposes a novel task, concept-map-based multi-document summarization (MDS), arguing that concept maps offer a more intuitive and structured summary format aligned with human information-seeking behavior than traditional text summaries. To enable research in this new paradigm, the authors introduce a comprehensive corpus creation methodology. This multi-stage process integrates automatic Open Information Extraction (Open IE) for initial proposition generation, a novel 'low-context importance annotation' crowdsourcing scheme for efficient importance scoring of propositions, and expert annotation for final concept map construction and refinement. A key feature of the created corpus is its scale and heterogeneity, comprising 30 topics with large, diverse web document clusters, significantly surpassing traditional summarization datasets. The paper also provides a baseline system and an evaluation protocol, aiming to establish a foundation for future research in this distinct summarization approach.
specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper introduces concept-map-based multi-document summarization (MDS) and a new corpus to support this novel task. The core reasoning is that concept maps offer a valuable, structured summary format, and a hybrid corpus creation method (automatic extraction, 'low-context' crowdsourcing, expert annotation) can efficiently build a high-quality dataset. Most claims regarding the novelty of the task, the creation of the corpus, its characteristics, and the reliability of expert annotation are well-supported by direct evidence within the manuscript. However, claims about the 'low-context importance annotation' scheme fully resolving prior quality issues or working 'reasonably well' are partially supported or overstated, as the evidence primarily demonstrates reliability and utility in a different context (TAC documents) or relies on preliminary tests and specific conditions. The effectiveness of the SVM classifier for proposition filtering is also partially supported, as it relies on manual verification for a subset of classifications. The overall methodology is sound for the expert-driven stages, but the validity and generalizability of the low-context crowdsourcing without full document context remain areas of concern, despite its demonstrated reliability in pilot studies.

Instead, the low-context design fundamentally changes the task, potentially circumventing these issues rather than resolving them in a comparable setting. The propositions themselves must be sufficiently self-contained such that their importance can be reliably assessed in isolation, or the relative importance ranking must be robust even if absolute importance is difficult to gauge without full context.

The subsequent expert annotation and revision stages must be robust enough to identify and correct any systematic biases or errors introduced by the low-context crowdsourcing, ensuring the high quality of the final gold-standard concept maps.

consensus_findings: The paper proposes a novel task: concept-map-based multi-document summarization (MDS), addressing a clear gap in existing resources for structured summarization outputs.

A new, large-scale, and heterogeneous corpus has been created and released, featuring document clusters 15 times larger and more diverse than typical DUC/TAC clusters, posing a challenging summarization task.

The corpus creation methodology is a systematic, multi-stage pipeline combining automatic preprocessing (Open IE), a novel 'low-context importance annotation' crowdsourcing scheme, and high-quality expert annotations.

The expert annotation stages for concept map construction (proposition selection, concept joining, concept labeling) demonstrate substantial inter-annotator agreement (Kappa values 0.66-0.70), providing robust evidence for the quality of the final gold-standard concept maps.
The 'low-context importance annotation' crowdsourcing scheme demonstrates reliability and consistency in its annotations, as evidenced by pilot studies and application to the new dataset.

The released corpus, along with a baseline system and proposed evaluation protocol, is publicly available, which is highly beneficial for promoting reproducibility and enabling further research in this new area.

Analysis of the baseline system effectively reveals major bottlenecks and challenges for concept-map-based MDS, particularly in content selection and relation extraction, highlighting the task's complexity.
disagreements: There is a controlled disagreement regarding the *type* of novelty: some reviewers emphasize the 'disruptive' nature of re-framing MDS output to concept maps and the unconventional 'low-context' crowdsourcing, while others highlight the 'incremental' refinement of existing practices and extension of the summarization paradigm. However, all acknowledge the paper's significant contribution to novelty.

Reviewers consistently raise concerns about the *validity* of the 'low-context importance annotation' without full document context. While the method's *reliability* is demonstrated, the *methodology_auditor* and *claim_verifier* more directly question its *accuracy* and *validity* for truly reflecting document-specific importance, whereas *novelty_assessors* frame this as an inherent 'novelty risk' of a pioneering approach.

All reviewers identify an inconsistency between the paper's stated focus on an 'extractive variant' of the task and the allowance for 'up to three synthetic relations' (making maps 'slightly abstractive') in the expert-created gold standard. This is framed as a 'methodological flaw' or 'inconsistency' by some and a 'novelty risk' or 'conceptual tension' by others.
uncertainty_hotspots: The effectiveness of the 'low-context' crowdsourcing design relies on workers' ability to relate to the topic without full document context, which might vary and is not fully quantified.

The claim that 'low-context importance annotation' resolves quality issues from prior work (Lloret et al., 2013) is not directly supported by evidence of resolution in the same context, but rather by a change in task design, introducing uncertainty about direct comparability.

The SVM classifier for proposition filtering was tuned to avoid false negatives, which might lead to a higher fraction of positive classifications requiring manual verification, indicating a limitation in full automation and conditional effectiveness.

Manual correction was performed for 'least confident negative classifications' and 'positive classifications for certain types of tuples' where the classifier was imprecise, highlighting the limits of the automatic filtering and the reliance on manual intervention.
The allowance for 'up to three synthetic relations' makes the maps 'slightly abstractive', which introduces a tension with the stated focus on an 'extractive variant' for automatic evaluation.

The proposed automatic evaluation measures (Strict Match, METEOR, ROUGE-2) 'might be complemented with a human evaluation', indicating that their comprehensiveness or validity might be limited on their own for structured concept map outputs.

The claim that the low-context design works 'reasonably well' is based on 'preliminary tests' and is conditional on the topic being 'relatable to the worker', which introduces a degree of subjectivity and potential variability not fully quantified.

The generalizability of the crowdsourcing reliability results (from TAC documents) to the new corpus's larger, more heterogeneous web document clusters is assumed rather than explicitly re-validated for accuracy.
The long-term impact and adoption of concept-map-based MDS as a primary summarization output format are yet to be seen.
The generalizability of the 'low-context' crowdsourcing approach to other complex tasks without significant loss of quality needs further exploration.

The choice of selecting the top 50 propositions per topic for expert annotation appears to be an arbitrary threshold, lacking a strong justification for its optimality in terms of summary completeness or conciseness.
model_diversity_effects: The *structure_analyst* (reviewer_1) provided a high-level assessment of the logical coherence of the paper's argument, identifying strengths in systematic construction and robust validation, and highlighting inconsistencies as methodological flaws.

The *methodology_auditor* (reviewer_2) rigorously scrutinized the reproducibility and validity of the methods, raising the 'low-context' annotation's *validity* (accuracy) as a major concern, distinct from its demonstrated *reliability* (consistency). This role also emphasized the inconsistency in task definition and limitations of evaluation metrics as methodological flaws.

The *novelty_assessor_incremental* (reviewer_3) focused on how the paper refines existing practices and extends the MDS task, framing concerns (e.g., low-context nuance, extractive/abstractive inconsistency) as 'novelty risks' inherent to innovative approaches, rather than outright flaws.

The *novelty_assessor_disruptive* (reviewer_4) emphasized the fundamental re-framing of summarization output and the unconventional data creation methodology as highly disruptive. Similar concerns were also framed as 'novelty risks,' highlighting the inherent risks of pioneering new approaches.

The *claim_verifier* (reviewer_5) systematically checked claims against evidence, identifying where claims were strongly supported, partially supported, or overstated, providing granular uncertainty flags for specific claims, particularly regarding the 'low-context' crowdsourcing and SVM filtering.

This diversity of cognitive roles ensured a comprehensive assessment, exploring both the innovative aspects and the potential weaknesses/risks of the methodology from multiple perspectives, distinguishing between novelty, methodological soundness, and evidence-based support.
meta_review.editor_guidance: The editor should request a clear and unambiguous definition of the concept-map-based MDS task, specifically addressing the tension between the stated 'extractive variant' and the 'slightly abstractive' elements in the gold standard. Further empirical validation or a more robust theoretical justification for the *validity* (accuracy, not just reliability) of the 'low-context importance annotation' without full document context is crucial. The paper should expand on the limitations of the proposed automatic evaluation metrics and suggest more comprehensive structural/semantic metrics or a plan for human evaluation. Additionally, more thorough documentation of manual intervention steps in proposition filtering, including effort and inter-annotator agreement, and a stronger rationale for arbitrary thresholds like the selection of 50 propositions, would be beneficial.
meta_review.author_guidance: Authors should clarify the precise definition of the concept-map-based MDS task, either by strictly enforcing a purely extractive gold standard or by explicitly defining it as a 'hybrid extractive-abstractive' task and discussing the implications for evaluation. To address concerns about the 'low-context importance annotation', conduct a targeted study comparing low-context crowd judgments with expert judgments made with full document context for a subset of propositions to validate accuracy. Provide a more robust theoretical or empirical justification for the 'low-context' approach's validity and discuss how it addresses or avoids prior crowdsourcing issues. Enhance the evaluation protocol by discussing the specific limitations of current automatic metrics and suggesting concrete directions for future human evaluation or more sophisticated structural/semantic metrics. Provide more details on the manual verification and correction process for proposition filtering, including inter-annotator agreement and total effort. Offer a stronger rationale or sensitivity analysis for the choice of 50 propositions for expert annotation. Finally, address the generalizability of the crowdsourcing pilot study to the new corpus's heterogeneous web documents and discuss the long-term implications of Open IE's limitations on concept map quality.

The limitations and trade-offs of the crowdsourcing scheme, such as the 'low-context' design and the cost of comparison tasks, are explicitly mentioned.
The tuning strategy for the SVM classifier, prioritizing false negative avoidance and acknowledging the need for manual verification, is transparently discussed.
Inter-annotator agreement scores are provided for both crowdsourcing pilot studies and expert annotation steps, enhancing confidence in data quality.

epistemic_limits: The analysis is based solely on the provided paper context and specialist reviews; no external information or direct interaction with the authors was possible.

The assessment of 'validity' for the 'low-context importance annotation' is challenging without ground truth comparisons (e.g., expert annotations with full context). The reviews primarily assess *reliability* (consistency) rather than *accuracy* (correspondence to true importance).
The long-term impact and adoption of concept-map-based MDS as a primary summarization output format are yet to be seen and cannot be fully assessed at this stage.
The generalizability of the 'low-context' crowdsourcing approach to other complex tasks or less 'relatable' topics without significant loss of quality needs further empirical exploration.
The assessment of the 'disruptive' vs. 'incremental' nature of the novelty involves subjective interpretation, even with defined lenses.
The effectiveness of the proposed automatic evaluation metrics for capturing the full quality of structured concept maps is inherently limited and acknowledged by the paper itself.
The analysis of potential biases introduced by manual intervention steps (e.g., SVM filtering corrections) is limited by the level of detail provided in the paper regarding these processes.
The counterfactual conditions for success, while insightful, are speculative and depend on future research and empirical findings.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: been intensively studied and is well represented in research literature. We report related work in the Section 2.1. Text summarisation, after Mani ( 1999), is the process of “taking an information source, extracting content from it, and presenting the most important content to the user [...]. Summaries can be user-focused [...] tailored to the requirements of a particular user or group of users, or else, they can be generic, i.e., aimed at a particular – usually broad – readership community.”. The GES problem studied in this paper can be viewed as a generic type of summarisation i.e. aimed at a broad group of users with various information needs for whom the particular task is not known. Of course, GES is not the same problem as text summarisation, but the analogies are obvious and we build the concept of GES on those analogies. Mani (1999) further distinguishes between extractive and abstractive summaries. The former one is more basic and is achieved by simply selecting (extracting) the elements, typically sentences, from the summarised text to present them as the summary. The latter one, more sophisticated, is capable of synthesising new elements out of the summarised text. The GES problem naturally corresponds to the extractive generic summarisation as it selects s-p-o triples from the underlying knowledge graph to compose the resulting graphical summary

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Text summarisation, after Mani ( 1999), is the process of “taking an information source, extracting content from it, and presenting the most important content to the user [...]. Summaries can be user-focused [...] tailored to the requirements of a particular user or group of users, or else, they can be generic, i.e., aimed at a particular – usually broad – readership community.”. The GES problem studied in this paper can be viewed as a generic type of summarisation i.e. aimed at a broad group of users with various information needs for whom the particular task is not known. Of course, GES is not the same problem as text summarisation, but the analogies are obvious and we build the concept of GES on those analogies. Mani (1999) further distinguishes between extractive and abstractive summaries. The former one is more basic and is achieved by simply selecting (extracting) the elements, typically sentences, from the summarised text to present them as the summary. The latter one, more sophisticated, is capable of synthesising new elements out of the summarised text. The GES problem naturally corresponds to the extractive generic summarisation as it selects s-p-o triples from the underlying knowledge graph to compose the resulting graphical summary

Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review.
